headline: ADI设机器人初创陪跑平台，能否补上量产断层
lead: 机器人初创企业在传感、运动控制和AI上往往跑得很快，却在电子、系统集成、验证与制造环节卡住。ADI把Emerging Tech Hub放进Analog Garage，试图以弹性工程支持和制造资源弥合这段断层，但能否真正帮企业规模化，还取决于资源如何匹配不同阶段的需求。

chapters.title: ADI设机器人初创陪跑平台，能否补上量产断层
chapters.angle: 机器人初创企业在传感、运动控制和AI上往往跑得很快，却在电子、系统集成、验证与制造环节卡住。ADI把Emerging Tech Hub放进Analog Garage，试图以弹性工程支持和制造资源弥合这段断层，但能否真正帮企业规模化，还取决于资源如何匹配不同阶段的需求。

sentences.text: ADI高级产品技术经理卡梅伦·维隆把机器人初创企业当下最大的挑战归结为行业变化的速度。
在他看来，多数初创企业擅长采用传感、运动控制和AI等新一代技术，但商业化还需要电子、系统集成、验证和制造方面的额外专业能力。
这些需求往往会拉紧张小型工程团队的资源。
ADI正在Analog Garage内发展Emerging Tech Hub，面向机器人初创企业和成熟公司，帮助它们应对上述挑战。
据该机构披露，这个中心意在让企业在把设计推向生产前，获得ADI工程师、原型设计与测试资源以及制造和采购方面的专业能力。

blocks.text: ADI高级产品技术经理卡梅伦·维隆把机器人初创企业当下最大的挑战归结为行业变化的速度。在他看来，多数初创企业擅长采用传感、运动控制和AI等新一代技术，但商业化还需要电子、系统集成、验证和制造方面的额外专业能力。这些需求往往会拉紧张小型工程团队的资源。ADI正在Analog Garage内发展Emerging Tech Hub，面向机器人初创企业和成熟公司，帮助它们应对上述挑战。据该机构披露，这个中心意在让企业在把设计推向生产前，获得ADI工程师、原型设计与测试资源以及制造和采购方面的专业能力。

sentences.text: Emerging Tech Hub被描述为一个聚焦机器人的计划，目标是把初创公司和成熟机器人企业拉近到ADI的技术团队，其中包括正在落地新发布或仍在开发中的技术的工程师。
ADI提供的工程支持将取决于机器人公司所处的阶段和具体需求。
例如，一家成熟机器人开发商可能需要某种特定的半导体元器件，另一家可能在解决不同的工程问题，Emerging Tech Hub便会在ADI内部寻找相应的专家。
维隆表示，ADI已从行业各处招募机器人专家，以便更好地应对快节奏的机器人开发。
ADI此前在一份白皮书中把物理AI描述为把传感、信号转换、感知、推理、控制、计算和验证结合在一起，并把它分为创意、原型、验证和规模化四个阶段。
ADI称，机器人初创企业不断变化的需求，正是Emerging Tech Hub想要填补的缺口。

sentences.text: 从机制上看，ADI要兜住的不是单点技术，而是从创意到规模化之间的工程化断层。
依据是ADI自己把物理AI拆成创意、原型、验证和规模化四个阶段，又承认初创企业在电子、系统集成、验证和制造上需要额外专业能力，这说明断层主要出在跨学科整合，而非算法或传感本身。
但这种模式的约束同样来自阶段差异：支持内容取决于企业所处阶段和需求，成熟开发商可能只要一颗特定元器件，另一家可能要解决完全不同的工程问题，这意味着中心更像一个按需求调配专家的接口，而不是一条标准化的量产服务流水线。
因此它能否奏效，关键不在于工程师数量，而在于匹配效率：若每次需求都要在ADI内部临时寻找专家，规模化的边际成本可能偏高。

sentences.text: 与单纯提供芯片或参考设计相比，这个中心把原型设计和测试资源、制造与采购经验一并打包，试图覆盖更长的链条。
而ADI此前通过白皮书给出的四阶段框架，为这种打包提供了叙事框架，但框架本身并不等于资源已经到位，两者之间仍有待验证的距离。
据该机构披露，ADI从行业各处招募机器人专家，这更像是试图补上系统集成和验证能力的组织性做法，而非仅靠原有半导体团队承接。

sentences.text: 我们的判断是，Emerging Tech Hub切中的是真实痛点，但材料只披露了正在发展和计划中的安排，尚未给出已有企业落地量产的案例或量化结果，因此它目前更接近一个有依据的方向，而不是已被验证的解药。
接下来可观察两点：是否公布参与企业从原型或验证阶段进入规模化的具体进展；以及ADI内部专家匹配是按项目临时响应，还是形成了可复用的支持流程。
第三点观察制造和采购资源是否有可核对的落地动作，而非停留在能力描述。

evidenceRecords.text: “The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI).

In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing.
These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams.
ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges.
The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production.

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation.
ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale.
These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address.

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies.
The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs.

For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI.
Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development.

history.title: Crew-12 set to depart the ISS after eighth months in orbit
history.originalTitle: Crew-12 set to depart the ISS after eighth months in orbit

evidenceRecords.text: After eight months aboard the International Space Station, NASA and SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission is scheduled to undock from the Station’s Harmony port on Oct. 7 to return to Earth.
Undocking and landing Crew-12 is scheduled to undock from the International Space Station’s (ISS) Harmony zenith port on Wednesday, Oct. 7, at 12:05 UTC (08:05 EDT).

Crew-12’s crew spent their last days on the Station preparing for their return, packing essential items, testing their SpaceX pressure suits, and preparing the Station for the arrival of their follow-up mission, Crew-13.
Expedition 75 crew members onboard the Station will then work to ensure Crew-12 can safely undock from the ISS, checking pressure values and hatch seals.
The crew of Crew-12 don their SpaceX pressure suits in preparation for undocking.
Crew-12 launched to the ISS on Feb. 13 from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
Crew-12’s return was greenlit by the arrival of Crew-13 on Oct. 1 at 23:05 UTC.
Crew-12 marks Crew Dragon Freedom’s fifth mission overall, following Crew-4, Crew-9, Axiom-2, and Axiom-3.
When Freedom splashes down with Crew-12, it will have spent a total of 609 days and 11 hours in space.
Crew-12 launches to the ISS. (Credit: Max Evans for NSF) Crew-12’s busy mission During the crew’s stay aboard the ISS, they worked as part of ISS Expeditions 74 and 75.

See Also Crew-12 Updates ISS Forum Section NSF Store Click here to Join L2 During the Crew 12’s eight-month stay, Meir and Adenot completed four extravehicular activities (EVAs), or spacewalks, to conduct vital station maintenance outside the orbiting laboratory.
While aboard the @Space_Station , Crew-12 contributed to science research including studying cancer-targeting treatments, bone loss and regeneration, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

history.title: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations
history.originalTitle: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations

evidenceRecords.text: Credit: NASA NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit.
On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations.

“In alignment with the President’s National Space Policy, NASA is committed to maintaining a sustained American presence in low Earth orbit long after the International Space Station retires,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.” Building on the agency’s Ignition event earlier this year, NASA regularly has engaged with private industry to shape the agency’s future direction in low Earth orbit.
This included publishing two Requests for Information in March to gather industry’s perspective on low Earth orbit destinations and transportation.

The agency also published a draft Request for Proposals in July, followed by an industry day and one-on-one meetings that allowed interested companies to review and comment on the planned acquisition approach.
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” said Isaacman.
“Since Ignition, we have spent a lot of time listening to industry and working through what it will take to make this transition successful.

We want to see credible plans, strong technical execution, and companies prepared to invest in destinations that can serve NASA while developing additional customers and markets of their own.” Proposals are due Tuesday, Dec. 8, with contract awards expected in spring 2027.

Learn more about NASA’s missions on the agency’s website: https://www.nasa.gov -end- George Alderman / Joshua Finch Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 george.c.alderman@nasa.gov / joshua.a.finch@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Oct 09, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Commercial Space Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate Low Earth Orbit Economy

history.title: Honda Wants to Put a Robotic Lab Assistant on Future Commercial Space Stations
history.originalTitle: Honda Wants to Put a Robotic Lab Assistant on Future Commercial Space Stations

evidenceRecords.text: Now, it’s teaming up with space infrastructure firm Redwire to develop an automated laboratory support system for use on future commercial space stations.
As I’m writing this I’m able to stare out into my driveway at my trusty Honda Odyssey.
Most of the public’s association with Honda is through their “mobility” products - i.e. their cars.
But the company has an impressive track record of other technical achievements, not the least of which has been in robotics.
Automation will undoubtedly play a major role in future space stations, and Honda / Redwire’s offering sounds appealing with its impressive technical capabilities.
But it remains to be seen if that is what the burgeoning space automation industry will rally around, or whether another option would potentially better fit the bill.
But as space becomes more commercial, competition to supply the “shovels” of the next round of microgravity scientific research will undoubtedly heat up.

evidenceRecords.text: “The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI).

In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing.
These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams.
ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges.
The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production.

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation.
ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale.
These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address.

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies.
The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs.

For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI.
Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development.

history.title: Crew-12 set to depart the ISS after eighth months in orbit
history.originalTitle: Crew-12 set to depart the ISS after eighth months in orbit

evidenceRecords.text: After eight months aboard the International Space Station, NASA and SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission is scheduled to undock from the Station’s Harmony port on Oct. 7 to return to Earth.
Undocking and landing Crew-12 is scheduled to undock from the International Space Station’s (ISS) Harmony zenith port on Wednesday, Oct. 7, at 12:05 UTC (08:05 EDT).

Crew-12’s crew spent their last days on the Station preparing for their return, packing essential items, testing their SpaceX pressure suits, and preparing the Station for the arrival of their follow-up mission, Crew-13.
Expedition 75 crew members onboard the Station will then work to ensure Crew-12 can safely undock from the ISS, checking pressure values and hatch seals.
The crew of Crew-12 don their SpaceX pressure suits in preparation for undocking.
Crew-12 launched to the ISS on Feb. 13 from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
Crew-12’s return was greenlit by the arrival of Crew-13 on Oct. 1 at 23:05 UTC.
Crew-12 marks Crew Dragon Freedom’s fifth mission overall, following Crew-4, Crew-9, Axiom-2, and Axiom-3.
When Freedom splashes down with Crew-12, it will have spent a total of 609 days and 11 hours in space.
Crew-12 launches to the ISS. (Credit: Max Evans for NSF) Crew-12’s busy mission During the crew’s stay aboard the ISS, they worked as part of ISS Expeditions 74 and 75.

See Also Crew-12 Updates ISS Forum Section NSF Store Click here to Join L2 During the Crew 12’s eight-month stay, Meir and Adenot completed four extravehicular activities (EVAs), or spacewalks, to conduct vital station maintenance outside the orbiting laboratory.
While aboard the @Space_Station , Crew-12 contributed to science research including studying cancer-targeting treatments, bone loss and regeneration, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

history.title: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations
history.originalTitle: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations

evidenceRecords.text: Credit: NASA NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit.
On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations.

“In alignment with the President’s National Space Policy, NASA is committed to maintaining a sustained American presence in low Earth orbit long after the International Space Station retires,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.” Building on the agency’s Ignition event earlier this year, NASA regularly has engaged with private industry to shape the agency’s future direction in low Earth orbit.
This included publishing two Requests for Information in March to gather industry’s perspective on low Earth orbit destinations and transportation.

The agency also published a draft Request for Proposals in July, followed by an industry day and one-on-one meetings that allowed interested companies to review and comment on the planned acquisition approach.
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” said Isaacman.
“Since Ignition, we have spent a lot of time listening to industry and working through what it will take to make this transition successful.

We want to see credible plans, strong technical execution, and companies prepared to invest in destinations that can serve NASA while developing additional customers and markets of their own.” Proposals are due Tuesday, Dec. 8, with contract awards expected in spring 2027.

evidenceRecords.text: Now, it’s teaming up with space infrastructure firm Redwire to develop an automated laboratory support system for use on future commercial space stations.
As I’m writing this I’m able to stare out into my driveway at my trusty Honda Odyssey.
Most of the public’s association with Honda is through their “mobility” products - i.e. their cars.
But the company has an impressive track record of other technical achievements, not the least of which has been in robotics.
Automation will undoubtedly play a major role in future space stations, and Honda / Redwire’s offering sounds appealing with its impressive technical capabilities.
But it remains to be seen if that is what the burgeoning space automation industry will rally around, or whether another option would potentially better fit the bill.
But as space becomes more commercial, competition to supply the “shovels” of the next round of microgravity scientific research will undoubtedly heat up.
